title: The mirror
hookLine: to young Rahula: reflect as in a mirror before speaking or acting (MN 61)

lines: A SEAT AND A VESSEL OF WATER.
A LITTLE LEFT IN THE BOTTOM.
cards: Late afternoon, at Ambalatthika, near Rajagaha. A boy named Rahula sees his father coming and sets out a seat and a vessel of water for washing feet. The father is the Buddha.

Rahula is his son, now a novice monk, and tradition says he was about seven. The Buddha washes his feet and leaves a little water in the bottom of the vessel. Rahula, do you see this little bit of water?
Yes, sir. That little, he says, is what's left of the monk's life in anyone who feels no shame telling a deliberate lie. He throws the water away.
Then he turns the vessel upside down.

teach.b: It's a stark start for a seven-year-old, and it begins with lying for a reason: someone with no shame about a deliberate lie, the Buddha says, could do any wrong at all. Then he changes the picture.
Rahula, what is a mirror for? For reflecting, sir. In the same way, he says, reflect before you do anything with your body, your speech or your mind.
Would this lead to harm for me, for others, or for both? If so, don't do it. If not, go ahead.

Reflect while you're doing it too, and stop if you see harm. And reflect afterward. If a word or deed turned out harmful, he tells his son, reveal it to a teacher or a wise companion, and hold back next time.
If it turned out well, be glad, and keep training. For a harmful thought, be troubled by it and turn away.
Before, during, after: three looks in the mirror, at three doors, body, speech and mind. Notice the tone. There's no threat of punishment.
A child is handed a tool, not a lecture, and a mirror is a gentle tool. It doesn't scold. It just shows you your face.
The teaching even ends with gladness: when you see you've done well, enjoy it.
For speech, the mirror is a pause.
One breath between the thought and the sentence, long enough to ask: who will this help, and who could it hurt?

how: Many Buddhists use this teaching as a daily review: reflecting before acting, and in the evening looking back over the day's words and deeds; in monasteries, faults are acknowledged to a fellow monastic.

o: a way of seeing your past lives
a symbol of vanity and self-admiration
reflecting before, during and after you act

games.q: what happens at Ambalatthika: tap the pairs.
p: the Buddha's son, a young novice
reveal it, and hold back next time

s: the mirror teaching is only about looking before you act
MN 61 says reflect before, during and after, in body, speech and mind.
tradition says Rahula was about seven when he heard this
the commentary puts his age at seven.
the teaching ends with a threat of punishment
it tells him to be glad when he sees he has done well.

games.q: you're Rahula. you realize something you said yesterday hurt a friend. what does your father tell you to do?
o: forget it; it's in the past.
reveal it to a teacher or wise friend, and hold back next time.
games.why: in MN 61 the Buddha tells Rahula to reveal a harmful word or deed to the teacher or wise companions and to restrain himself in future; for a good one, to be glad.

practice: Picture a small mirror in your hand, and hold up to it something you're likely to say today, an email, a reply, a comment at dinner: will it harm me, them, or both?
Then look again at something you said yesterday, gently, the way a mirror looks, without scolding. If it went well, let yourself be glad; if it didn't, note it, and set it down.

wordCard.voice: The mirror. The Buddha's tool for his son Rahula: reflect before, during and after acting, in body, speech and mind.

orig.note: Pali ādāsa: mirror. 'What is a mirror for?' 'For reflecting, sir.'

carryVoice: Your line: look in the mirror. The glass is there before, during and after. Day three hundred sixty-eight, complete.
